title: Chapter 6 — Of The Progress Of Roman Catholicism In The United States
paragraphs: America is the most democratic country in the world, and at the same time — according to credible reports — the country in which the Roman Catholic religion is making the most progress. At first glance this is surprising. Two things must be carefully distinguished here: equality inclines people to want to form their own opinions, but on the other hand it fills them with a taste and an idea of unity, simplicity, and impartiality in the power that governs society. People living in democratic ages are therefore very prone to throw off all religious authority; but if they consent to submit themselves to any authority of this kind, they prefer at least that it be single and uniform. Religious powers that do not radiate from a common center are naturally repugnant to their minds, and they can almost as easily conceive of there being no religion as of there being several. Today, more than in any previous age, Roman Catholics are seen lapsing into unbelief, and Protestants converting to Roman Catholicism. If the Roman Catholic faith is considered within the bounds of the church, it seems to be losing ground; beyond those bounds, it seems to be gaining. Nor is this circumstance difficult to explain. The people of our time are naturally disposed to believe; but as soon as they have any religion, they immediately find in themselves a latent tendency that pushes them unconsciously toward Catholicism. Many of the doctrines and practices of the Church of Rome astonish them, yet they feel a secret admiration for its discipline, and its great unity attracts them. If Catholicism could eventually withdraw from the political animosities it has provoked, I have little doubt that the same spirit of the age which now appears so opposed to it would become so favorable as to permit its great and sudden advance. One of the most ordinary weaknesses of the human mind is to try to reconcile contrary principles, and to buy peace at the expense of logic. Thus there have always been, and always will be, people who, after submitting some portion of their religious belief to the principle of authority, try to exempt several other parts of their faith from its influence, and keep their minds drifting at random between liberty and obedience. But I am inclined to believe that the number of such thinkers will be smaller in democratic ages than in others, and that our descendants will tend more and more to divide into two camps — some abandoning Christianity entirely, and others returning to the bosom of the Church of Rome.
